newsitem.title: USA: Introducing teenage girls to entrepreneurship.
newsitem.headline: Introducing teenage girls to entrepreneurship.

text.p: Victoria Groves just finished her freshman year at the University of Massachusetts, writes for the college newspaper and hopes to become a political journalist in Washington. But in the back of her mind lurks the knowledge that if she opts to become an entrepreneur, she'll be prepared.

Groves, 18, was the winner -- for the second consecutive year -- of the National Business Plan Competition, created by "An Income of Her Own," a non-profit organisation that aims to help teenage girls achieve economic self-reliance by introducing them to the fundamentals of business.
Her latest winning plan was for "Notetakers," a professional note-taking service for college students.

Like many ideas for new businesses, her's was not entirely original. With 30,000 students at the university and as many as 100 people in a large lecture class, people who cannot make it to class still need the notes. In fact, there is another note-taking service on campus.
"The changes I made were putting the service in a more central location, and I was going to lower my prices and pay the students more to take notes," said Groves.

Now that she's home on vacation in Chelmsford, Mass., Groves is keeping busy with her previous business, a desk-top publishing venture she developed while a junior in high school. She's working on revising a menu for a diner in nearby Lowell, Mass.

"The women who own their own companies have spoken with us in "An Income of Her Own" about the difficulty of starting up your own company," said Groves. "What they're trying to teach us is that if we have the drive and the motivation, we can achieve whatever we want to achieve.
"If that's running a business, we can be successful at that. We learn that you have to take care of the people who are trusting you -- your employees and your customers -- and the money will come."

Joline Godfrey, who founded the non-profit group in 1992, says young women need to learn that business is relevant to them. "Girls still don't hear the message: 'You can own the whole show,'" she said. "We wanted to offer that message."

Godfrey is the author of two books on entrepreneurship for women: "Our Wildest Dreams: Women Entrepreneurs Making Money, Having Fun, Doing Good" and "No More Frogs to Kiss: 99 Ways to Give Economic Power to Girls."

"Teens who complete our programmes may or may not start their own businesses," said Godfrey. "But we hope they will have greater confidence in their own creativity and intelligence, continue their education and build on the knowledge gained in our programmes as a foundation for a strong, economically secure life."

In addition to the business plan competition, the Santa Barbara, Calif.-based group offers one-day conferences across the country, runs startup camps in California, New Mexico and Massachusetts and works with after-school programmes and local girls clubs. It also offers games and other informational material on its website.

"In any one of those activities, girls will have access to meeting other business women, do activities that are hands-on and uncover their own entrepreneural spirit," said Godfrey. "They will learn that ownership is an option -- not just of a business, but having stocks and bonds, or even a patent."

The business plan competition started four years ago. "When we did a conference, at the end of the day, the teenagers would say: 'This is cool. Now what?'" said Godfrey. "We created the business plan contest to make sure we had a followup activity."

The group holds 15 to 20 one-day conferences around the country annually and hopes to double that in 1998. They are usually on a school day or a Saturday, for a minimum of 50 girls and a maximum of 125.

It also runs training programmes to teach others how to do the one-day conferences in their communities. It frequently receives requests for conference help from local women's business organisations or parent-teacher associations.

At Camp Startup, a two-week summer residential programme, girls work together to learn to create a business plan. "It's fun for them in that not only are they creating a business plan, but they get to meet some of the country's leading women business owners," Godfrey said. "We try to make sure the girls meet women who own different-sized companies, from various industries."

For example, she related, last year, after listening to the owner of a winery discuss her business experience, one girl said: "This is really neat. I love science, but I never realised that this is what I could do with it."
For more information, contact "An Income of Her Own" at 800-350-2978 or via its website at www.anincomeofherown.com.
